blocks.text: On Linux, published-port traffic is DNAT'd in PREROUTING and forwarded through the FORWARD chain, never touching INPUT, where UFW and most host firewall rules live, so `ufw deny` doesn't protect published container ports.

$ sudo ufw deny 5432
$ docker run -d -p 5432:5432 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=weak postgres:17
# port 5432 is still open to the internet

blocks.src: generate: Packet flow: incoming packet → PREROUTING (Docker DNAT) → FORWARD (DOCKER-USER → DOCKER) → container; separate path → INPUT (ufw) → host processes; highlight that published ports skip INPUT
blocks.alt: Why ufw rules don't apply to published ports.
blocks.caption: Why ufw rules don't apply to published ports.

items: Don't publish internal services; containers talk over Docker networks.
Bind loopback: `-p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432` (use an SSH tunnel for remote tools).
Rules in `DOCKER-USER`, which Docker creates, leaves alone, and evaluates first.
An external firewall or cloud security group.
ufw-docker to integrate UFW with DOCKER-USER.

blocks.text: Don't set `"iptables": false` in daemon.json. It breaks NAT, publishing and network isolation.

Q: "You blocked 5432 with ufw but the Postgres container is reachable from the internet. Why?" A: "Docker's DNAT sends published traffic through the FORWARD chain, bypassing ufw's INPUT rules, and -p binds 0.0.0.0. Don't publish it, or bind 127.0.0.1, and enforce filtering in DOCKER-USER or an external firewall."
